name: Meditation / mindfulness
lead: Meditation and mindfulness are attention-training practices used for stress management and emotional regulation. In clinical psychology, mindfulness is deliberate, usually nonjudgmental awareness of bodily sensations, feelings, thoughts and surroundings.[1] In appearance and self-improvement communities it is discussed as a way to reduce stress and improve self-image.

Research on meditation is large but methodologically uneven: a 2012 meta-analysis excluded almost three quarters of 595 identified studies for methodological problems,[2] and a 2007 evidence review described the state of research across practices.[3] No studies in the sources reviewed test meditation for physical appearance.

paras: The term mindfulness comes from the Pali word sati; modern Western practice draws mainly on Zen and Theravada-based vipassana.[1] Herbert Benson brought relaxation-based techniques into Western medicine in 1975, Jon Kabat-Zinn founded Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction in 1979, and Segal and Williams later developed Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy.[1] Mindfulness expanded into schools, workplaces and apps, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic.[1]

A 2009 study comparing experienced meditators with meditation-naive controls reported better attentional performance and cognitive flexibility among meditators.[4] A 2015 randomised trial of 75 volunteers reported that mindfulness meditation reduced pain through mechanisms different from placebo.[5] A 2012 review of MBSR, MBCT and Zen meditation examined depression, anxiety, pain and distress,[6] a 2013 review examined stress-management programmes for medical students,[7] and a 2021 study examined mindfulness for stress and burnout in nurses.[8] A 2009 review assessed sitting-meditation interventions in youth.[9]

Wikipedia reports that MBCT was designed to prevent depression relapse and that research found roughly 50 percent reduced relapse in people with three or more prior episodes; school reviews found small, mostly short-term improvements, while an earlier review by Johnson and colleagues (2016) found no measurable gains.[1]

Early research was criticised for weak methods and inconsistent definitions, and some scholars argue psychology narrows mindfulness to attention and drops its ethical components; the 'McMindfulness' critique holds that commercialisation turns it into a productivity product.[1]
Studies listed above address stress, pain, attention, depression and anxiety in general and special populations.[2][3][5][6][7][8] No studies found that test meditation for appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Herbert Benson introduces relaxation techniques to Western medicine.[1]

card.summary: Attention-training practice used for stress and self-image; broad stress research exists, but none on appearance.
card.note: Research quality is uneven; no studies test appearance outcomes.

quick.overview:
Meditation and mindfulness train attention and non-judgmental awareness, and are used in looksmaxxing circles to manage stress and self-image.

Reviews report benefits for stress, pain and mood in some populations, though a 2012 meta-analysis noted that methodological problems excluded most studies.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners focus attention on breath, body or thoughts without judgement; studies suggest effects on attention and pain processing distinct from placebo.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed document no physical risks. Critics note commercialisation and inconsistent definitions, and no studies test appearance outcomes.
